Where a prescription becomes an order

Designing MedQuest OMS — the system that has to hold hands with the patient app on one side and the pharmacy's physical stock on the other, then survive contact with a live pharmacy floor.

9→1manual steps collapsed into one pipeline
10→1clicks per address label
30 minto first trial-run halt · 23 Jul 2026
Liverolled out at the PFC post-trial fixes
01 — Problem statement

An order that lives in nobody's system

Today, when a patient pays for medication in the Doctor Anywhere app, that order is immediately orphaned. It leaves the app as a PDF, lands in a pharmacy fulfilment centre (PFC) transcriber's inbox, gets copy-pasted into a spreadsheet, printed, walked across a room three times, and only becomes "real" again — reflected in stock counts — once someone has manually re-typed it a fourth time into a completely separate inventory tool.

Nobody owns the order between payment and delivery. The patient app knows it was paid for. The PFC floor knows it physically happened. Inventory (IMS) only finds out once a human decides to tell it. MedQuest OMS exists to close that gap — to give the order a single digital record from PAID to COMPLETED — without duplicating what the patient app already owns (payment, identity) or what IMS already owns (stock truth, batches, expiry).

That framing matters for scope: OMS is connective tissue, not a third source of truth. Every design decision below is really a decision about where OMS's authority ends and a neighbouring system's begins.

Companion case study This is part one. The inventory side of the same platform — the system that becomes the single source of truth OMS reads from — is IMS: One record, every pharmacy →
02 — My role

Senior Product Designer, owning both ends

I joined mid-refinement, after the previous designer had left — and inherited two systems at once: OMS already in flight toward a July trial, IMS still being scoped out of four disconnected legacy tools. My job was making sure neither one drifted from the reality of the PFC floor or the Marina Health warehouse.

Concretely, that meant:

  • Research, first-hand. Ran the onboarding whiteboarding session that mapped the PFC's physical production line station by station, and reviewed the Marina Health config admin's Friday configuration cycle end to end.
  • Design ownership across both systems. Designed OMS's order lifecycle, pack/validate flows, and label printing from scratch; led IMS's Item Master, Pricing Schemes, and Pharmacies modules through 90/80/70% completion.
  • Design QA. Audited the existing OMS Figma file against the PRD and filed DD-2817 — 17 issues, each with a node link and a fix, including the Packing-state action bug that would otherwise have shipped wrong.
  • Present at the point of failure. Authored the UAT Testing Guide, was on the floor for the 23 July trial run, and wrote up all five findings the same day — two of which trace back to a data gap, not a screen.
  • Cross-team translation. Sat between the PM, engineering, PFC/business stakeholders, and the separate Marina Health/IMS team — the two systems only work if the contract between them (the batch-deduction event) is something both sides actually agreed to.
03 — Sequencing

Why OMS shipped first, and IMS follows

Both systems were needed. Only one could go first, and the choice wasn't arbitrary — it followed from where the pain was most acute and how cleanly each system's scope could be isolated from the other.

Ships first — OMS

Urgent, visible, patient-facing

Every order was already a 9-step manual relay with no digital record between payment and delivery. The pain was immediate, the fix was scoped to one team (PFC), and the IMS dependency could be reduced to a single event contract — the batch deduction fired at VALIDATED — so OMS never had to wait on IMS's own timeline.

Follows — IMS

Foundational, cross-org, longer runway

IMS has to retire four systems (Excel, AP1, Plato, and eventually feed Provider Web) across 13 locations and two teams that had never had to agree on a shared record before. That's a bigger blast radius — deliberately phased into Phase 1 (configuration, now in engineering build) and Phase 1B (live stock, FEFO) after.

The PRD made this sequencing explicit: OMS's own spec marks the IMS deduction story "FYI US — NOT TO DO." OMS only has to fire the event and show a batch-number field — that scope cut is what let OMS reach a live pharmacy floor while IMS was still being scoped.

05 — Prioritization

What made the cut, and why

Every open item across both systems gets ranked against the same four questions — not a workshop exercise, the actual filter used on the backlogs in this case study.

Critical
Does it block go-live, or did it already cause a trial to fail?The Packing-state action bug. The medication-label data gap that halted the 23 July trial in 30 minutes.
High
Is it frequent, and does it touch compliance or patient safety?The missing Plato sync-failure indicator. The free-text batch number with no IMS validation behind it.
Medium
Does it improve clarity without blocking anything?The dashboard's missing auto-refresh signal. Renaming an ambiguous button label.
Deferred
Is it real, but explicitly out of scope for this phase?FEFO batch deduction, real-time stock-on-hand — both scoped to IMS Phase 1B on purpose, not dropped.
06 — What's at stake

What happens if we don't build either one

Neither system is a nice-to-have. Here's what stays true if OMS and IMS don't ship.

Without OMS
  • Fulfilment stays capped by transcriber headcount — a 9-step manual relay can't absorb more patient volume without adding people.
  • Every wrong label is a live dispensing risk, not a caught trial finding — FIND-02 almost went out on a patient's order.
  • No digital record exists between payment and delivery — nothing to audit if a complaint or a compliance review comes in.
Without IMS
  • The Marina Health config admin stays the single point of failure for 400+ SKUs across 13 locations — all of it in one head, none of it backed up.
  • Every new drug or price change stays an 8x manual edit — the bottleneck that caps how fast Marina Health can react to formulary changes.
  • OMS's batch-number field stays free text indefinitely — the one seam between "packed" and "correctly stocked" is never actually validated.
07 — The patient's view

One journey, and the silence in the middle

OMS never renders a screen a patient sees — but everything it does happens inside their experience. Mapping the journey from the end of the video consult to the medicine at the door made one thing obvious: the longest, most anxious stretch is "PFC packing," where the patient has zero visibility. That's precisely the stretch OMS governs.

The anxiety peak sits at stage 05, PFC packing — no channel is visible to the patient while the order is picked, packed, and validated. It's the strongest argument for the "your order is being packed" notification in the opportunities row, and the reason OMS's internal states need to be legible enough to drive one.

08 — Before & after

The manual line OMS replaces, step for step

The current fulfilment process is a nine-step relay of email, PDF, printouts, Plato, and a shared Excel file — documented station by station during onboarding. OMS doesn't reinvent the physical floor; it replaces each manual ritual with one digital equivalent.

Today — manual, 9 steps
OMS — one pipeline
Step 1 · TranscriberOpen the order email, copy 10–15 orders into a personal folder (15–20 at peak).Feels like: guessing, no undo
Job poolOrders arrive digitally and rank themselves by delivery window — no inbox, no folders.Feels like: nothing to lose track of
Steps 2–4 · PrintingPrint the medication page, copy-paste the address into a sticker format (10 clicks), print the medication label from Plato.Feels like: repetitive, one typo from a wrong label
One-click printConsolidated + individual lists, delivery and medication labels print together from the order — the address label is one click, not ten.Feels like: the same correct label, every time
Steps 5–6 · Pick & trayPicker pulls medicine for the batch; transcriber consolidates labels into a tray.Feels like: trusting the tray, not the record
Consolidated picking listOne list of every SKU across the batch with quantities, so the picker pulls from the shelf once.Feels like: knowing what's short before you start
Steps 7–8 · Pack & checkPacker sorts each order into its own bag with address + barcode; checker double-checks patient details and medications.Feels like: checking a printout against a bag, hoping nothing shifted
Order detailsEvery order's contents, patient, and state on one screen — the checker verifies against the record, not a printout.Feels like: match or no match — no guessing

09 — The three systems

One order, three owners, one handshake

The cleanest way the team found to talk about scope: IMS owns the physical. OMS owns the order. They meet exactly once, at the moment a Checker validates a packed order.

Patient app
DA VC · payment, identity
order created
OMS
order lifecycle, fulfilment, delivery
at VALIDATED
IMS
Marina team · SKUs, batches, stock
IMS owns the physical. OMS owns the order. They meet at one moment: VALIDATED.Working principle, IMS ↔ OMS integration notes

When an order reaches VALIDATED — meaning a Checker has physically verified the packed bag — OMS fires a batch-level deduction event outward. Nothing earlier: if an order is cancelled or split before validation, IMS never hears about it, so stock always reflects what was actually packed, not what was planned.

OMS order → VALIDATED ↓ IMS receives deduction event · SKU ID · Batch number · Quantity ↓ IMS reduces stock for those batches
Scope guardrail The inventory deduction story is marked "FYI US — NOT TO DO" in the OMS PRD. OMS triggers the event; IMS's own PRD defines what happens after. Practically: OMS's UI never shows stock levels or batch availability — the only visible touchpoint is a single Batch Number field on Order Details, currently free text.
10 — The physical floor

A day at the PFC, station by station

Before any of this is a screen, it's a conveyor belt of people. Orders move left to right across four roles, and OMS's job at each station is to replace one specific paper-and-Excel ritual — not to redesign the floor.

Station 1

Transcriber

Receives orders as email PDFs, copies them into a personal folder, prints medication + address labels by hand.

Pain10 clicks to copy-paste one address label from PDF to sticker format.
Station 2

Picker

Pulls physical medication off shelves for a batch of ~10 orders at once, using a printed pack list.

PainNo consolidated view — quantities are tallied by hand across orders.
Station 3

Labeller

Takes the picked medication and per-order labels, packs each order into its own bag individually.

PainWhich printed document belongs to which station is tribal knowledge.
Station 4

Checker / Validator

Verifies medicine, quantity, and patient details match; ticks a paper checklist; scans the order ID into Excel.

PainNo feedback loop — nothing confirms a scan succeeded or how many orders are left.

11 — Order lifecycle

Every order's path, and its one detour

OMS models the order as a small state machine. Five states are the happy path; one, Pending Clarification, is the escape hatch every exception routes through — and the only state where an order can be edited, cancelled, or split.

PAID
→
PENDING PACKING
→
PACKING
→
VALIDATED
→
COMPLETED
PAID
→
⟲ PENDING CLARIFICATION
→
CANCELLED

Pending Packing, Packing, and Validated can all route into Pending Clarification; "Clarified" always returns the order to its exact previous state — never a fresh one.

Paid

Created the instant the patient app confirms payment. View-only until it enters the job pool.

Pending Packing

Sits in a queue ranked by delivery-window end time. "Pack Next N" assigns a batch to a PFC Ops user.

Packing

Assigned and being physically packed. Only path forward is Validated (or Clarification).

Validated

Checker has scanned and confirmed. Fires the IMS deduction event and the Plato clinical sync in the same breath.

Pending Clarification

Exception state with a reason code (stock issue, prescription issue, patient request…). Slack-notifies every PFC Ops user.

Completed / Cancelled

Terminal. Completed requires a delivery-partner confirmation via RIDA — never a manual click.

13 — Contact with reality

The trial run — 23 July 2026

Design survives exactly until it meets a real pharmacy floor. On 23 July, OMS went into a live production trial at the PFC. These are photos from that morning — the system genuinely running, orders on the screen, the TSC label printer wired in, a picker at the bins.

Halted · 30 min
The trial run was stopped within 30 minutes. No orders were successfully packed. Root cause: critical printing errors in the Consolidated Packing List and Medication Labels. It was, bluntly, a failure — and the most useful half hour in the project so far. Five findings came out of it, each now traced to a specific gap.
FIND-02 · Pack orders — Medication LabelsCritical
The label printed one sticker per tablet, not one per pack
What happened
For an order of 10 tablets, the system printed 10 individual medication labels instead of 1 for the pack. Significant label waste; the output couldn't be used.
Expected
One medication label per SKU line, with the quantity stated on it ("10 tablets").
Root cause
The quantity_per_label per-SKU config isn't implemented correctly — and the ~400-SKU UOM→label-quantity mapping (the PFC business stakeholder / CS team) hadn't been delivered to engineering. A data gap, surfacing as a printing bug.
FIND-01 · Consolidated Packing ListLow
Quantities and units on the picking list didn't match the order
What happened
The printed Consolidated Packing List showed wrong quantities and units of measure — "1 bottle" where it should read "1 tablet." Pickers couldn't tell what to pull from the shelf.
Expected
Correct quantity and UOM per SKU, so a picker knows exactly what to pull.
Root cause
Same missing UOM→label mapping as FIND-02. The list renders whatever quantity_per_label holds — and for most SKUs it was blank or wrong.
FIND-03 · Print action, all label typesCritical
Nothing in OMS told the picker whether printing had finished
What happened
After sending order-barcode labels to print, the picker had no confirmation in OMS. They watched the physical printer and the screen at the same time, unsure which would tell them it was done. No success state, no printed count, no error if it failed.
Expected
A clear print confirmation — job sent, how many labels, success or failure — so the picker never has to watch the printer to know OMS is finished.
Root cause
No print-confirmation state was designed for any of the five document types; the Print control has no loading, success, or error state (also logged as design-audit Issue #13, wrong component for the Print action).
FIND-04 · DashboardLow
Managers kept hammering "refresh"
What happened
With no visible signal that auto-refresh was running, managers clicked the manual refresh button over and over. Only a static "Last updated" timestamp — no interval, countdown, or animation.
Fix
Remove the manual button; add an "Auto-refreshes every 60s" label and a live "Updated Xs ago" counter. A post-launch polish item, not a blocker.
FIND-05 · Pack Next NPRD decision
"Pack Next 10" mixed delivery slots together
What happened
Pack Next N assigns the 10 most urgent orders across all slots, so a batch mixed 2PM, 4PM, and 6PM windows. But the floor works one slot at a time.
Open decision
Should Pack Next N be slot-filtered, or stay a cross-slot priority queue? Either way the delivery slot must be visible per row. Escalated to the PM — a PRD-level call, not a pure design fix.
What the trial actually proved Four of the five findings trace to two upstream gaps, not screen design: the missing 400-SKU label-quantity data (FIND-01, FIND-02) and undesigned system-feedback states (FIND-03, FIND-04). The floor didn't reject the workflow — it rejected shipping before the label data and the print/refresh feedback states were done. That's a far cheaper lesson at 30 minutes than at go-live.
14 — Business impact

What this actually buys the business

Translated out of UX metrics: OMS removes the operational ceiling on how many orders the PFC can fulfil without adding headcount, and turns every dispensing error the trial run caught into a caught bug instead of a patient incident. IMS removes the Marina Health config admin as the single point of failure for the medication catalogue the entire patient app depends on, and cuts the time to add or reprice a drug from a multi-day manual sweep down to one edit.

9→1manual steps per order — PFC throughput stops scaling 1:1 with headcount
400+SKUs that stop depending on one person's memory and a Friday afternoon
8→1edits to change one drug's price across every pharmacy — fewer chances for a pricing error to reach a patient's bill
2critical printing gaps caught in a 30-minute trial, not after go-live — the whole point of piloting before scaling

Neither number is a projection. OMS is mid-rollout and IMS is now in engineering build — every figure above is the direct, traceable consequence of a specific pain point fixed above, not a forecast.

16 — The cross-team seam

The trust gap between OMS and IMS

IMS and OMS are built by two different teams that have never had to fully agree on a contract. Today the entire handshake rests on one editable text field.

Edit risk PFC Ops can hand-edit the Batch Number field on Order Details while an order is in Pending Clarification — and it's currently free text, unvalidated against IMS's actual batch records. A typo deducts the wrong batch from stock, silently. OMS already applies FEFO (nearest-expiry) logic, so it usually knows the right answer; the open question is whether a human override should bypass that without a check.
Continues in part two The batch records this field should validate against, the FEFO deduction that consumes this event, and the Marina team who own it are all the subject of the companion study — IMS: One record, every pharmacy →
